title: How AI is changing the role of economists
gist: Oxford Economics' CEO argues AI won't replace economists but will absorb repetitive forecast-checking and QA work, freeing economists to focus on judgement and interpretation as information becomes commoditised; the firm is embedding its research into client AI workflows via tools like AskOEAI and an MCP integration.

themes.theme: AI absorbs quality-assurance work rather than replacing economists

insights.claim: AI will not replace economists, but it creates an opportunity for economists to refocus their time on the highest-value parts of the job rather than repetitive forecast-checking.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Signals that professional-services firms expect AI to reshape internal workflows and staffing allocation before it displaces headcount, relevant for assessing AI's near-term labor impact on analyst-heavy industries.
insights.quote: AI will not replace economists. It does, however, give us an opportunity to refocus where we add the greatest value.
insights.locator: As an economist and CEO, I've been reflecting on what AI means

insights.claim: Unlike traditional automated checks that only flag forecasts against fixed thresholds, AI-based quality assurance can review thousands of forecasts simultaneously, detect unusual patterns, and surface recurring issues that rule-based systems would miss.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A concrete, already-deployed use case of AI in forecast validation at a major macro research house, useful as a benchmark for how AI is operationalised in research/analytics workflows rather than just chatbots.
insights.quote: It can review thousands of forecasts simultaneously, identify unusual patterns, recognise inconsistencies that warrant further investigation and provide economists with another set of eyes before analysis reaches clients.
insights.locator: This is where AI is already delivering tangible value

themes.theme: As information becomes abundant, judgement becomes the scarce and valuable asset

insights.claim: As generative AI makes information retrieval and summarisation abundant and cheap, the scarce and valuable resource shifts to interpretation: knowing what matters, what happens next, and how to respond.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for valuing knowledge-work businesses in an AI-abundant world: commoditised information access compresses margins for pure aggregators while rewarding firms that sell judgement and interpretation.
insights.quote: As information becomes more abundant, the insights that help answer those questions become more valuable.
insights.locator: In a world where information becomes abundant, what becomes scarce?

insights.claim: The author defines good economics as exercising judgement, challenging assumptions, interpreting conflicting evidence, and identifying signals others have not yet recognised, not simply retrieving or restating known facts.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Useful benchmark for distinguishing AI-substitutable analyst tasks (retrieval, restating) from durable human-value tasks (judgement, contrarian signal-spotting) when evaluating which knowledge jobs are at risk.
insights.quote: Good economics has never been about simply retrieving or restating what is already known. It is about exercising judgement, challenging assumptions, interpreting conflicting evidence and identifying signals that others have not yet recognised.
insights.locator: The economist's job is evolving, and that should excite us

insights.claim: The firm views AI as increasing the urgency, not just the opportunity, for economists to invest development time in judgement, rigorous analysis, and clear communication rather than treating these as a leisurely long-term goal.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Suggests firms in research/advisory sectors will accelerate reskilling and hiring toward judgement-heavy roles sooner than previously planned, a trend investors in professional-services and ed/training could watch.
insights.quote: What AI changes is the opportunity, and perhaps the urgency, to focus more of our time and development on those capabilities.
insights.locator: None of that is new. In fact, it is what we have always expected

themes.theme: Productising proprietary research as an AI-native distribution moat

insights.claim: Oxford Economics has built new tools, AskOEAI and an integration with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), to let clients access the firm's research and insights directly within their own AI tools and workflows.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that data/research vendors are racing to become MCP-accessible data sources for enterprise AI agents; a template for how B2B research providers monetise via AI-native distribution rather than just reports.
insights.quote: New tools we built such as AskOEAI and our integration with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are helping our clients access our insights more naturally within their existing AI tools and workflows.
insights.locator: AI now gives us new ways to deliver that expertise

insights.claim: The firm argues that the value of AI-delivered research tools still depends entirely on the depth of human expertise, testing, and training behind them, positioning proprietary human research as the durable moat even as delivery becomes AI-mediated.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Counters the narrative that AI commoditises research entirely; implies incumbents with deep proprietary datasets and analyst expertise can defend pricing power by wrapping that expertise in AI interfaces rather than being disintermediated by generic LLMs.
insights.quote: Behind every AskOEAI answer sits years of research, along with months of testing and training by our economists to ensure the outputs are accurate, grounded in evidence and worthy of our clients' trust.
insights.locator: But the quality of what those tools deliver still depends
